# Prime factors with SagePod

This notebook checks a finite factorization alongside a reading of Euclid's
argument that there are infinitely many primes. Open the [source overview](overview.md)
for the source passage and its MRW retained-outline reference. The transcription's
translator and edition are unknown.

The independently known product $3 \cdot 11 \cdot 31 = 1023$ gives the check
$$2^{10}-1 = 1023 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 31.$$
The factors are prime: trial division by primes at most their square roots suffices.
This example does not prove the general result in Euclid IX.20.

from sage.env import SAGE_VERSION
import sys, os
from pathlib import Path
from IPython import get_ipython
print("SageMath:", SAGE_VERSION)
print("Kernel:", type(get_ipython()).__module__)
print("Python:", sys.version.split()[0])
print("Container working directory:", Path.cwd())
print("Kernel PID:", os.getpid())
print("Prior calculation in live memory:", isinstance(globals().get("n"), Integer))

n = 2^10 - 1
factors = factor(n)
assert n == 1023
assert factors.prod() == 3 * 11 * 31 == n
assert list(factors) == [(3, 1), (11, 1), (31, 1)]
print("2^10 - 1 =", n)
print("Prime factorization:", factors)
print("Independent product:", 3 * 11 * 31)

## Continuing later
